phonemes.desc: The Old Norse diphthong ei, [ɛi]: a glide opening at the short front vowel of 'bed' and closing toward 'ee' — one syllable, never two.
The trilled nominative ending [r], lightly sounded, as in modern Icelandic Eir.

pronunciation.approximation: 'AYR' — one syllable: glide from the e of 'bed' into 'ee', and close with a light trilled r; modern Icelanders say it nearly the same way.

kin.label: Old Norse
kin.form: Eir, third of the ásynjur in Snorri's catalogue; the common noun eir means 'help, mercy, clemency'.

kin.label: Younger Futhark
kin.form: ᛅᛁᚱ (a-i-r) — the ᛁ rune writes both e and i; a normalized rendering, not an attested carving.

kin.label: Modern Icelandic
kin.form: Eir, an unbroken living given name; the verb eira, 'to spare, show mercy', keeps the noun's family alive.

pronunciation.note: Eir is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter — so the ASCII alphabet loses nothing in copying it. Three letters and a capital; the goddess's standing in the sources is entirely beside the orthographic point.

domains.title: Healing, Mercy, Medical Skill
domains.subtitle: The Best Physician of the Ásynjur
domains.lead: Eir is the Norse tradition's one physician: third in Snorri's catalogue of the ásynjur, defined by a single superlative — læknir beztr, 'the best of healers' — and named again among the healing maidens of Lyfjaberg in Fjölsvinnsmál. Her name is the common noun for mercy itself.

cards.name: Lyfjaberg
cards.desc: The 'mountain of healing' where Menglöð sits with her maidens — lyf is the Old Norse word for medicinal herbs and remedies.

cards.name: The Nine Maidens
cards.desc: Hlíf, Hlífþursa, Þjóðvarta, Björt, Blíð, Blíðr, Fríð, Eir, and Aurboða — the company Fjölsviðr names at Menglöð's knees.

cards.name: The Holy Place
cards.desc: Fjölsvinnsmál's promise: the maidens protect those who make offering at the sacred stead, and no sickness shall drag them down.

cards.name: The Superlative
cards.desc: Læknir beztr — 'the best physician': the only office Snorri gives her, and the only medical title in the ásynjur catalogue.

symbols.name: Lyfjaberg
symbols.meaning: The mountain of remedies — healing made landscape, the high place where help is found

symbols.name: The nine maidens
symbols.meaning: Protection, brightness, joy, mercy: the named company whose gifts are the inventory of recovery

symbols.name: The altar at the holy place
symbols.meaning: The covenant of Fjölsvinnsmál — sacrifice answered with deliverance from sickness

symbols.name: Menglöð's knee
symbols.meaning: The healing maidens sit at the necklace-glad one's knees — mercy attendant upon splendour

symbols.name: The name itself
symbols.meaning: Eir, 'help, mercy': the remedy and the plea for it in a single word

mythology.lead: Eir has the thinnest dossier of any goddess in the Edda — one superlative in Snorri's catalogue and one stanza-list in the Poetic Edda — and the office both witnesses agree on: she heals. Nothing else about her was ever written down.

myths.title: The Best Physician
myths.text: Snorri's catalogue of the ásynjur runs like a court roll: Frigg is highest; second is Sága at Søkkvabekkr; and then, without genealogy, marriage, or adventure, the third entry: 'Eir is the third: she is the best physician' — Eir er þriðja: hon er læknir beztr. That is the whole notice. No hall is named, no parentage given, no deed narrated. In a catalogue that finds something to say about every goddess — Fulla's headband, Gefjun's plough, Syn's door-keeping — Eir alone is defined by a profession and a superlative, and the profession is medicine.

myths.title: The Maidens of Lyfjaberg
myths.text: The Poetic Edda keeps her second witness in the strangest of its love-quests. Svipdagr, come to win Menglöð, must answer the gate-ward Fjölsviðr riddle for riddle; among his questions is this: what are the maids called who sit at Menglöð's knees in harmony together? Fjölsviðr names nine: Hlíf the protectress, Hlífþursa, Þjóðvarta, Björt the bright, Blíð and Blíðr the blithe, Fríð the fair, Eir, and Aurboða. Then comes the promise that makes the list matter: these maidens will give help if men make offering at the holy place, and no sickness so cruel will seize the sons of men that they cannot free them from it. Menglöð's seat is Lyfjaberg, the mountain of healing — and Eir, 'mercy', stands named in its company.

myths.title: Valkyrie and Kenning
myths.text: The name has a quieter afterlife in the poets' apparatus. The þulur — the metrical name-lists preserved with the Prose Edda — count an Eir among the valkyries, and the skalds used eir as a base-word in kennings for women, as the handbooks register: 'Eir of the ale' or 'Eir of rings' is simply a woman, any goddess's name being lawful tender in the kenning system. Whether the valkyrie Eir is the physician of Gylfaginning under another aspect or a second bearer of the name, the sources do not say; Simek registers the double attestation and leaves the door open. What the kennings prove is that the name lived in the working memory of the poets.

myths.title: The Menglöð Question
myths.text: Who is the lady of Lyfjaberg whom Eir attends? Menglöð — 'the one gladdened by necklaces' — bears a name that points straight at Freyja, owner of the Brísingamen, and much scholarship has taken Menglöð as a byname or hypostasis of the Vanadís rather than a separate figure; the two poems of Svipdagsmál as a whole have often been read as a fragmentary Freyja-myth. The identification is attractive and unprovable, and the cautious handbooks present it as exactly that. If it holds, then the North's one physician sits in Freyja's own retinue — mercy among the attendants of love; if it does not, Lyfjaberg keeps its own mistress, and Eir keeps hers.

lore.syncretism: No interpretatio romana ever found Eir a Latin name: the classical authors who mapped the northern gods left her unmentioned, and the medieval Icelandic writers who knew her wrote no equation. Her real company is native. The Germanic world knew healing as a craft guarded by female figures and spoken charms — the Second Merseburg Charm, the one surviving Old High German healing spell with divine names, binds Wodan and the healing of a wrenched foot in a formula that has Norse echoes, and the Edda's own Oddrúnargrátr gives a mortal woman, Oddrún, the role of birth-helper 'come from the southland'. Eir is the divine end of that continuum: the household of healing maidens on Lyfjaberg raised to the rank of ásynja. Modern comparisons with Greek healing deities are analogies of office, not borrowings — the name eir is transparently Norse, the common noun for mercy, and the tradition grew its physician out of its own vocabulary of help.
lore.culturalLegacy: Eir's afterlife is quiet and remarkably alive. The name never died in the North: Eir remains a living Icelandic given name, and its family survives in the everyday verb eira, 'to spare, to show mercy'. Modern Heathen and Ásatrú practice, which keeps few of the lesser ásynjur in regular use, has made room for her precisely because her office is the one every household needs — she is invoked in healing rites as the physician Snorri named. Popular culture reached her through the valkyrie list: an Eir numbered among the valkyries appears in modern games and fiction, usually in the healer's role the þulur and Gylfaginning between them suggest. Her scholarly afterlife is disproportionate to her dossier: the two-sentence goddess of Gylfaginning 35 is the standing proof, cited in every handbook, that the Norse pantheon contained an explicit deity of medicine.
lore.extendedMeditation: Eir is the goddess made of a single word, and the word is mercy. The Edda gives her no story because her name is already the story: eir is what the wounded ask for and what the healer gives — help, clemency, the staying of a hand. Snorri places her third among the goddesses, ahead of figures with far longer dossiers, as if the catalogue itself understood that a pantheon without a physician would be incomplete. Fjölsvinnsmál completes the portrait by giving her a company and a mountain: mercy does not work alone but sits named among protection, brightness, gladness, and peace — the full inventory of what recovery feels like from the inside. To say her name in Old Norse was already to ask for the one thing medicine and prayer both promise.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Eir — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᛅᛁᚱ (a-i-r, the ᛁ rune writing both e and i, ᚱ the final nominative -r). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way long ago: eir.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Eir is an entirely textual goddess: no runestone invokes her, no votive deposit or place-name can be securely claimed for her, and no image is identified as hers. Her witnesses are manuscripts. The Gylfaginning notice survives with the Prose Edda — above all the Codex Regius (GKS 2367 4to, c. 1300) and its sister codices — while Fjölsvinnsmál hangs by a thinner thread: the poem is not in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda at all but is preserved only in seventeenth-century paper manuscripts, and it was nineteenth-century editors who first joined it with Grógaldr as the two halves of Svipdagsmál. The late transmission has made some scholars cautious about the poem's age, but its language and metre are accepted as medieval, and its Lyfjaberg catalogue remains the only narrative context in which the physician of the ásynjur is ever seen at her post.
